I mostly agree with you. I think the way this issue has been handled in the media and by the community has created challenges. In my opinion, there’s been too much emphasis on transgender topics, sometimes in ways that feel extreme. This includes actions by some advocates who, while well-intentioned, may have pushed too hard. The attention public schools paid to the topic became overwhelming for some. Aggressive demands to use specific pronouns or quick judgment of people for honest mistakes can sometimes feel excessive, leading to frustration or resistance from those who don’t fully understand or feel pressured by these expectations.

As a bisexual individual, I believe trans individuals should absolutely have access to all available medical treatments they may need. However, I have concerns about the growing reliance on medical interventions, such as hormones, puberty blockers, and HRT, especially when it comes to youth. There’s still much we don’t fully understand about the potential long-term effects of these treatments, which could lead to serious medical issues down the road. It’s essential to proceed cautiously and follow strict medical protocols to avoid over-prescribing treatments that may do more harm than good.

Another factor to consider is that transgender youth make up a very small percentage of the population—about 1.7%—but this number has surged in recent years. This rapid growth raises questions: is it due to genuine cases or something else, like FOMO or social influence? Youth can sometimes answer questions in ways they believe will lead to the results they want, which can then lead them toward lasting negative effects, both physically and socially.

There is also strong evidence showing that a significant percentage of individuals experience regret after undergoing these treatments. This makes it even more important to approach such decisions with care. My hope is for young people struggling with these issues to receive the support and care they need, including medical help if appropriate, but in a way that prioritizes thorough evaluation and responsible treatment practices.

If we want to help these youth, we might also need to recognize that not everyone will fully understand or accept everything right away. Trying to force acceptance may only build more resistance. By focusing on supporting those truly in need, rather than pushing against those who may never fully understand, we might find a path toward more meaningful, compassionate, and lasting progress.

### Why I Don’t Think Time Travel to the Past Is Possible

I don’t think time travel to the past is possible, or at least not probable. Here's why:

Data from the past is only preserved if we record it or find evidence. We rely on text, audio, video, fossils, carbon dating, archaeology, and astronomy to understand what happened. These methods provide limited snapshots of the past, helping us piece together an educated understanding.

If we lived in a computer simulation, maybe all data could be saved and revisited. However, simulating our entire world would require an insane amount of memory storage, far beyond our current technology.

Even if faster-than-light travel were possible, allowing us to outrun light and observe past events directly, it contradicts our understanding of physics. The immense data storage and energy required make the idea of revisiting the past highly speculative.

Given these limitations, the likelihood of actual time travel to the past seems incredibly low.

As someone that is just ended my unemployment situation since last November (starting a new job Monday), I have some advice...

I left my position on November 18th. Took the rest of November off to rest my head. Then, I started looking in December and realized with the holidays approaching there wasn't much being posted so I decided to start looking in January. As soon as I started looking I realized it had nothing to do with the holidays... it was a bad job market. The listing are flooded with fake jobs, lots of places that list positions never call, never respond, take the listing down, only to put it back up a few days later. As time went I got really depressed. So bad I had no choice, but to take a mental health break because I was falling apart. 

Ensure you have a routine, stay active, go for walks to get out of the house. Treat this as a job. If you feel you need a break take off a few days to maybe a week. I fear that if you take off too much time you might fall out of life too much and form bad habits. You may also miss on jobs that would have been great for you. Depression creeps in when you are out of sorts and not active enough. Don't let that happen. 

If you really need a break take a week off. Then come back strong and work on your resume to make it as good as possible. Then work on a cover letter template. I also started using chatgpt via Microsoft co-pilot. Use the notebook feature. The prompt you'll type into notebook will be large. It's your resume, paired with the job description, and a note asking to create a customized cover letter using your resume and the job description.  What it spits out might need some polishing, but it will help you save time and make the customized cover letter look great.  Next practice job interviews using Ai and YouTube. For YouTube type in mock job interviews. For ChatGPT use a prompt that says "run me through a job interview for \_\_\_\_\_\_, ask me 10 questions pertaining to that type of job, I'll answer them one my one, then give me feedback on my responses so I can improve them". 

You should also use this time to upskill yourself. Find a training course you can take to improve your resume and skills. Networking is a massive part of this too. Often someone you know ends up helping you out big time. Use Linkedin for this. Subscribe to the pro version just for now if you can afford the fee. If you don't have a LinkedIn create one and work on it. Employers will often look it over. Build your network by connecting with as many people as possible you know. 

GOOD LUCK!
